tips.title: Double consonants change the word
body: In Italian a double consonant is held a little longer, and it changes the meaning: nono (ninth), nonno (grandpa).
Listen for the tiny pause: sete (thirst) and sette (seven), pala (shovel) and palla (ball).

tips.title: Voglio il latte: Italian keeps “the”
body: Where English says “I want milk”, Italian usually keeps the article: voglio il latte, voglio il pane.
Asking politely, Italians say vorrei (I'd like): “Vorrei un caffè.”

tips.title: Il and la: every noun is masculine or feminine
body: Every Italian noun is masculine or feminine. “The” is il (masculine) or la (feminine); before a vowel both become l'.
Words in -o are usually masculine, in -a feminine, and in -e either: il cane (the dog), la notte (the night).

tips.title: No need for “he”, “she” or “I”
body: The verb ending says who is doing it, so io (I), lui (he) and lei (she) are usually left out: “Ho una sorella.”
È on its own means he is, she is or it is: “È mio fratello.” Family words drop the article: mio fratello, not il mio fratello.

tips.title: Adjectives go after the noun and match it
body: Most describing words come after the noun and change to match: piccolo / piccola, and for more than one piccoli / piccole.
A few common ones can go before: una bella casa, un buon caffè.

tips.title: Ho fame: Italian “has” hunger
body: To say you're hungry or sleepy, use avere (to have): ho fame, ho sonno.
The same goes for thirst (ho sete), cold (ho freddo) and heat (ho caldo).

tips.title: Voglio + a verb: “I want to…”
body: Put the verb straight after voglio: voglio giocare, “I want to play”. Vuoi is “you want”.
Non goes in front to say no: “Non voglio.”

tips.title: Mi piace works backwards
body: Mi piace means “it pleases me”: the thing you like is the subject. “Mi piace il cioccolato.”
For more than one thing, use piacciono: “Ti piacciono i cani?” (Do you like dogs?)

tips.title: Asking questions
body: A question is often the same sentence with a rising voice: “È vicino?” (Is it near?)
Question words: che cosa (what), chi (who), dove (where), perché (why), quanto (how much). Dove + è becomes dov'è.

tips.title: Su + il = sul: little words join up
body: In, su (on), di (of) and a (to) merge with the article: su + il = sul, in + la = nella, a + il = al.
“Il libro è sul tavolo”, “vado al parco”. They sound natural quickly.

tips.title: Telling someone what to do
body: For tu, the command is often the same as “he does”: gira (turn), vai (go), prendi (take).
To a stranger, use the polite Lei form: giri a sinistra, vada dritto.

tips.title: Essere or stare?
body: Essere is the main “to be”: sono insegnante, sono sposato.
Stare is for how you are: “Come stai?” “Sto bene.” It also means to stay: “Sto a casa.”

tips.title: Lei: the polite “you”
body: With strangers, shop staff and older people, Italians use Lei, which takes the same verb as “she”: “Ha un'altra taglia?”
Tu is for friends, family and people your age who've said so.
table: Tell me. (polite, how may I help?)

tips.title: Vorrei: a softer “I want”
body: Vorrei (I would like) is the polite way to order. “Voglio” can sound demanding.
“Per me…” (for me…) is the easy way to order: “Per me, il pollo.”

tips.title: Mi alzo: verbs you do to yourself
body: Some verbs come with mi, ti or si when you do them to yourself: mi alzo (I get up), mi vesto (I get dressed).
The mi goes right before the verb: “Mi chiamo Anna” (I call myself Anna).

tips.title: The past: ho mangiato, sono andato
body: The everyday past uses avere or essere + participle: ho mangiato (I ate), ho visto (I saw).
Verbs of movement and change take essere, and the ending matches: sono andato (a man), sono andata (a woman).

tips.title: Two past tenses: the scene and the event
body: The imperfect sets the scene or says what used to happen: abitava (she lived), andava (she would go).
Fairy tales tell the event with the passato remoto: trovò (she found). In speech you'd say “ha trovato”.

tips.title: Had done: era / aveva + participle
body: To say something had already happened, use the imperfect of avere or essere + participle: era andato via (had left), aveva mangiato (had eaten).
Mentre (while) + imperfect gives the background: “Mentre cucinavo, è squillato il telefono.”

tips.title: Plans: the present for the future
body: Italians often use the present for plans: “Prenoto un tavolo” (I'll book a table), “Ci vediamo alle otto.”
“Se piove, restiamo a casa”: se (if) + present, then present.

tips.title: Ho mal di… and mi fa male
body: “Ho mal di testa” (I have a headache), “ho mal di gola” (sore throat), “ho mal di pancia” (stomachache).
Pointing: “Mi fa male qui” (it hurts me here). Da means “since”: “la febbre da ieri”.

tips.title: Giving advice: dovresti, se fossi in te, and the subjunctive
body: “Dovresti…” (you should…) is gentle advice. “Se fossi in te…” (if I were you…) uses the imperfect subjunctive.
After “è importante che”, the verb goes into the subjunctive: “che tu beva”. “Ti consiglio di” takes a plain verb.

tips.title: È stato cancellato: the passive
body: Essere + participle says what was done to something: “Il volo è stato cancellato.”
The participle matches: la valigia è stata persa, i voli sono stati cancellati.

tips.title: Penso che + subjunctive
body: After penso che (I think that) and credo che, Italian uses the subjunctive: “Penso che tu abbia ragione.”
“Secondo me” (according to me) is the easy way to give an opinion with a normal verb: “Secondo me, è un errore.”

tips.title: Linking ideas
body: Da un lato… dall'altro… (on the one hand… on the other…) lays out two sides.
“Anche se” (even if) takes a normal verb: “Anche se è difficile.” “Tuttavia” means “however”.

tips.title: Tu or Lei?
body: Start with Lei with strangers, older people and at work. Friends, family and young people use tu.
“Possiamo darci del tu?” (can we use tu?) is the polite way to switch.
table: to use tu with each other

tips.title: Extra-polite requests
body: The conditional softens a request: potrebbe (could you), sarebbe (would it be), saprebbe (would you know).
“Mi saprebbe dire…?” (could you tell me…?) is a favorite polite opener.

tips.title: How people really talk
body: In speech, Italians drop and shorten words: “bella!” (hey friend!), “raga” (guys), “ci si becca” (see you around).
“Non mi va” (I don't feel like it) and “sono al verde” (I'm broke) are everyday phrases you'll hear all the time.

tips.title: Culture: dating in Italy
body: Italians tend to be expressive and complimentary. Going for an aperitivo (early-evening drinks with snacks) is the classic first date.
“Uscire con qualcuno” is to go out with someone; “stare insieme” means you're a couple.

tips.title: Culture: texting in Italy
body: Italians laugh in texts with “ahahah” or “ahah”. Voice notes on WhatsApp are everywhere.
Short forms: “cmq” (comunque, anyway), “nn” (non), “xké” (perché, why).

tips.title: Culture: meeting the family
body: Sunday lunch with the family can last hours. Bring a small gift (un pensierino), such as pastries from a pasticceria.
Use Lei with your partner's parents until they invite you to use tu, and compliment the cooking.

tips.title: Culture: Italian charm
body: Compliments are part of Italian charm: specific and sincere ones about style, a laugh or taste work best.
“Provarci” is to hit on someone. Keep it playful and respectful, and read the other person's reaction.

tips.title: Culture: teasing with style
body: Italians love friendly teasing (prendere in giro). A good comeback with a smile shows confidence.
“Se la tira” means someone's showing off: playful, not mean, between friends.

tips.title: Culture: clear and respectful
body: Ask clearly and take no for an answer. “Rispetto la tua risposta” shows respect.
“Nessun problema, è stato un piacere” ends things on a nice note.
table: Can I ask for your number?

tips.title: Culture: greetings in Italy
body: Friends greet with two kisses, starting on the left side. With strangers, a handshake and “Piacere”.
“Buongiorno” in the morning, “buonasera” from mid-afternoon. “Salve” is a safe, neutral hello.

tips.title: Culture: at the table in Italy
body: “Un caffè” is an espresso, drunk standing at the bar. Cappuccino is for the morning.
Pasta and meat come as separate courses (primo and secondo). The coperto, a small cover charge, is normal.

tips.title: Culture: holidays in Italy
body: At New Year (Capodanno) people eat lentils for money in the year ahead. On January 6 the Befana brings sweets, or coal to naughty children.
Ferragosto (August 15) is peak summer holiday: many shops close and cities empty out.

tips.title: Culture: mistakes foreigners make
body: False friends: parenti are relatives, camera is a room, morbido means soft, and “ho caldo” (not “sono caldo”) means you're hot.
Don't cut spaghetti with a knife, and think twice before asking for cheese on seafood pasta.

tips.title: Culture: dialects and regional slang
body: Italy is full of dialects. In Rome you'll hear “daje!” and “ammazza!”, in Naples “uè” and “guaglió”, in Sicily “mizzica!”.
Young people all over say “raga” (guys), “figo” (cool) and “che figata!”
